Chapter 9. Reflections on America.
As the years went by, my view of America kept expanding—growing both wider, and more personal. You know, the country that welcomed my family from Jamaica, offered us chances and challenges in equal measure, is still very much a work in progress.
I think about the journey from the Bronx all the way to the highest levels of leadership. It’s living proof of what’s possible here. But it’s also a reminder—there’s still so much left to do.
There are moments I’ll always be proud of. Times when this nation pulled together during a crisis. Or when everyday people stepped up in quiet, heroic ways. Then there’s the slow, steady march toward greater inclusion. But, there were also moments of real frustration. Divisions seemed to deepen. Old prejudices lingered, refusing to fade. And sometimes, it just felt like progress was always just out of reach.
When I sit down with young people, I hear the same questions over and over: Is the American dream still alive? Can anyone really make it? My answer—shaped by everything I’ve lived through—is both hopeful and honest. The path isn’t easy. The obstacles are real. But the promise of America? That belief that effort, character, and community can help you rise above your circumstances—that’s still worth holding on to.
It’s become clear to me that building a better country is never finished. Every generation faces its own challenges, its own tests of courage and compassion. The lesson I learned as a kid, and have seen proven again and again, is this: progress doesn’t depend on perfect leaders. It depends on ordinary people giving their best, day after day.
My story is just one thread in America’s larger tapestry. But it’s a reminder that, even when doubt and difficulty creep in, hope can still endure. And in the end, this journey—with all its twists and turns—really is worth taking.
